passages.t: The mountain of the LORD, and swords beaten into plowshares
passages.happening:
A new heading: ‘This is the message that was revealed to Isaiah son of Amoz concerning Judah and Jerusalem’ (verse 1).

‘In the last days the mountain of the house of the LORD will be established as the chief of the mountains; it will be raised above the hills, and all nations will stream to it’ (verse 2). Many peoples will say, come, let them go up to the house of the God of Jacob, so that he will teach them his ways. ‘For the law will go forth from Zion, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem’ (verse 3).

‘Then He will judge between the nations and arbitrate for many peoples. They will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation will no longer take up the sword against nation, nor train anymore for war’ (verse 4).

Then the invitation: ‘Come, O house of Jacob, let us walk in the light of the LORD’ (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 1 promised that Jerusalem would be purified and called the Faithful City. Chapter 2 paints that restored Jerusalem on a world scale. Not only Judah, but all nations, will come to Zion to be taught.

In the ancient world mountains were thought of as places where gods lived, and temples were often built on high places or designed as artificial mountains, like the ziggurats of Mesopotamia. Jerusalem's temple mount was not especially high. To picture it raised above all the hills was a statement about God, not about geography. And the picture of nations streaming to it reverses the story of Babel, where people gathered to build a tower and make a name for themselves.

The word for law, torah, means teaching or instruction. The nations come to Zion not to be conquered but to be taught. Swords and spears were costly iron weapons. Plowshares and pruning hooks were farm tools made from the same metal. To beat one into the other was to turn the resources of war into the resources of food.

These verses appear almost word for word in Micah 4, and scholars debate whether Isaiah borrowed from Micah, Micah from Isaiah, or both from an older song about Zion. There is no certain answer.
passages.later: Micah gives the same vision and adds a line: ‘each man will sit under his own vine and under his own fig tree, with no one to frighten him’ (Micah 4:4). The prophet Joel later turns the picture around in a call to battle: ‘Beat your plowshares into swords’ (Joel 3:10). And Peter, on the day of Pentecost, announces that ‘In the last days’ God is pouring out his Spirit (Acts 2:17).
passages.hard:
Is the vision of swords beaten into plowshares a hope for this age, or only for the age to come?

Readers differ. Some Christians read the passage as describing the present spread of the gospel, partly fulfilled wherever Christ's rule reconciles enemies, and draw from it a call to make peace now. Others, including many who expect a future earthly reign of Christ, read it as a promise for a coming age that human effort cannot bring about. Jewish interpreters have long read it as a hope of the Messiah still to come.

Most agree on two points. The passage makes peace flow from the nations learning God's ways, not from political arrangements alone. And verse 5, with its invitation to walk in that light now, suggests the vision was meant to shape present conduct as well as future hope. These notes take no side on how the vision will be fulfilled.
passages.asks: Isaiah sees the nations coming to learn God's ways, and then invites his own people to walk in that light now. Ask what it would look like for you to live by a promise that is not yet complete. And ask what weapons in your own life, words or habits or grudges, need beating into tools.

passages.t: A land full of silver, horses and idols
passages.happening:
Then Isaiah turns to Judah as it is. God has abandoned his people, ‘because they are filled with influences from the east; they are soothsayers like the Philistines’ (verse 6).

‘Their land is full of silver and gold, with no limit to their treasures; their land is full of horses, with no limit to their chariots’ (verse 7). ‘Their land is full of idols; they bow down to the work of their hands, to what their fingers have made’ (verse 8).

So mankind is brought low (verse 9). ‘Go into the rocks and hide in the dust from the terror of the LORD and the splendor of His majesty’ (verse 10). ‘The proud look of man will be humbled, and the loftiness of men brought low; the LORD alone will be exalted in that day’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The chapter reflects the prosperity of Judah in the eighth century BC, probably under Uzziah and Jotham, when the kingdom controlled trade routes, built fortifications, and gathered wealth and military strength. The silver, gold, horses and chariots of verse 7 are exactly what Deuteronomy warned a king not to multiply.

The influences from the east and the soothsaying like the Philistines point to foreign religious practices, especially divination, which came in along with trade and alliances. The idols Isaiah mocks were images of wood, stone or metal, often overlaid with silver or gold. The word he uses, elil, sounds like the word for God, but likely means something weak or worthless.

The contrast with verses 2 to 5 is sharp. The people who should be a light to the nations are copying them. The first hearers were living in good times, and Isaiah told them their good times were full of what God would bring down.
passages.later: Deuteronomy had warned that a king ‘must not acquire many horses for himself’ and ‘must not accumulate for himself large amounts of silver and gold’ (Deuteronomy 17:16-17).
passages.asks: Judah's land was full of silver, horses and idols, and all three were trusted. Ask what your life is full of, and what you lean on when you are afraid. And ask whether your prosperity has made you more like the nations or more like the light.

passages.t: The day of the LORD against all that is proud
passages.happening:
‘For the Day of the LORD of Hosts will come against all the proud and lofty’ (verse 12). It will come against the cedars of Lebanon and the oaks of Bashan (verse 13), against the tall mountains and high hills (verse 14), against every high tower and fortified wall (verse 15), against every ship of Tarshish and every stately vessel (verse 16).

‘So the pride of man will be brought low, and the loftiness of men will be humbled; the LORD alone will be exalted in that day, and the idols will vanish completely’ (verses 17-18).

People will flee to caves in the rocks and holes in the ground from the terror of the LORD, ‘when He rises to shake the earth’ (verse 19). In that day they will throw their idols of silver and gold to the moles and bats (verse 20).

The chapter ends with a blunt word: ‘Put no more trust in man, who has only the breath in his nostrils. Of what account is he?’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
The day of the LORD was a phrase the prophet Amos had already used, a day the people expected to bring victory and the prophets said would bring judgment on pride. Verses 12 to 16 are a list of ten lofty things, each introduced by against all, as if God were felling them one by one. The cedars of Lebanon and oaks of Bashan were the tallest and most prized trees of the region. Ships of Tarshish were large seagoing trading ships, named after a distant port whose location is uncertain, often identified with a site in Spain.

The chapter is built on repetition. The line that the LORD alone will be exalted in that day is its center. The flight into the rocks returns three times.

The idols thrown to the moles and bats are a sharp picture. What people made and worshiped will be tossed into the dark places where blind creatures live. And the last line turns from idols to people: do not put your trust in a mortal, whose life is only a breath.
passages.later: A psalm gives the same warning: ‘Put not your trust in princes, in mortal man, who cannot save’ (Psalm 146:3). And Revelation uses the same picture of people fleeing God's presence: the kings and the mighty ‘hid in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains’ (Revelation 6:15).
passages.asks: Everything tall in this chapter, trees, towers, ships, is brought low. Ask what you are proud of that God might bring down. And ask whom you are trusting who has only breath in his nostrils.
